subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning a module with a typewriter effect, sticking to safe, well-understood SDK methods rather than uncertain APIs. I'm thinking through how to orient cylinder parts correctly using the aim/dir/up options, since I'm not fully sure of their exact semantics.

For the key letters, I'm deciding between a canvas texture approach versus simpler geometric tricks, settling on small canvas textures per key with a dark disc and cream letter for reliability.

Now I'm sketching the overall dimensions: a compact typewriter body roughly 0.36 wide, with a sloped keyboard panel rising toward the back, staggered key rows, chrome rims around each key, and a lower green body shell forming the base structure.

Still writing geometry logic...

I'm working out the semicircle of bars forming the typebasket, placing each bar along a rim arc behind the keys and leaning them inward toward a central strike point, then adding a thin chrome torus arc to represent the type-segment guide, rotated into the correct plane.

I'm also positioning the black cylindrical platen above the bars and adjusting the convergence point where the bars meet, so their strike point sits just under the front of the platen.

Then I'm laying out the carriage frame with green end plates, chrome rail rods, platen knobs at the ends, and a chrome carriage return lever, fitting the overall body depth to around 0.45 units.

For the paper, I'm adding a thin tilted sheet standing behind the platen plus a curved partial-cylinder section wrapping over the platen's top surface to simulate paper feeding through.

I'm reconsidering the paper placement so the typed lines stay visible above the platen rather than hidden behind it, tilting the sheet slightly backward so the top passes over the roller without clipping into it.

Working out the geometry for the tilted sheet: computing its plane position relative to the platen using the normal and up vectors at a 20° tilt angle, then finding the sheet's center point and rotation needed so the top edge leans back.

Still working out local coordinates...

For the typed lines, I'm placing 8 rows of varying length near the lower half of the sheet, above where it contacts the platen, with a blank title line at top. I'm checking the geometry doesn't conflict with where the type bars converge toward the sheet.

Now I'm working out the keyboard bed as a sloped slab rising from front to back, computing the tilt angle and adjusting the slope ratio since my first attempt put the back edge too high.

I'm defining each key's geometry: a dark chrome stem rising from the bed, a chrome rim, and a cap disc with a cream letter rendered on a black background to simulate glass keycaps.

Now I'm working out the wedge beneath the keyboard bed, using an extruded shape to fill the sloped space from the base up to the key row, building it as a triangular prism extruded across the width.

I'm working out the wedge profile for the typewriter body, trying different coordinate options so the rear block height and bed step align properly with where the keys and rim meet.

Still working out the arc segment and bars geometry...

Checking the sheet's lowest point confirms it sits above the bar tips, which is good. Now I'm working out the carriage structure: platen end cheeks, chrome rail rod behind, green upright support posts at x ±0.2 spanning from the body deck to the carriage, and a cross bar beneath the platen to tie it together.

Still placing carriage parts...

Settling on a lever start position that clears the knob. Now I'm designing a brass badge plate for the front face with an inset line, tiny rivets, and a canvas-rendered text label like "MERIDIAN" positioned to face forward on the body.

I'm sizing the badge, then working out the chrome spacebar's position and dimensions relative to the keybed's sloped front edge, and laying out the key rows with proper stagger offsets and pitch spacing to mimic a real keyboard layout.

For keycaps, I'm planning circular tops with cream letters on dark glass-like material, and considering whether to use individual textures per key or build a shared atlas canvas with remapped UVs to keep things efficient.

I'm attaching the mesh to the base joint with the texture baked into the geometry, keeping a flat tilt. For color I'm picking a racing-green tone around #0b4d2e with shared glossy roughness across materials.

I'll traverse the model tree and adjust material properties by color match -- chrome parts get higher metalness and lower roughness, green parts get lower roughness, while textured meshes stay untouched. Chrome color is set to #d8dde0 with metalness .6 and roughness .25 to avoid looking too dark without an environment map, and the base gets small black cylindrical feet.

I'm adjusting the body profile so it starts slightly above zero with feet filling the gap underneath, adding a thin chrome trim strip along the front base, and adding a darker green plinth box for contrast at the base edges.

Now I'm positioning a pair of ribbon spool cylinders on the rear deck, checking their coordinates against the existing bars and uprights to avoid collisions, and nudging their placement inward to roughly ±.12 in x and -.225 in z so they clear the arc and corner posts.

Writing geometry helper functions...

Still writing helper functions...

For the paper sheet itself, I'm building a box geometry rotated to match the easel angle, colored like aged paper with dark ink text. I'm breaking typed lines into word-groups with random gaps to simulate typed text, spacing nine lines down the page with a left margin, and giving the first line a reddish heading color for variety.

I need to write my own simple random number generator since I'm unsure of the external rng API, then finalize the part counts for keys, bars, and letter meshes before writing the complete export code.

Working through the key stem geometry now — calculating the bed slab surface position per wedge angle, then stacking the stem cylinder, rim, cap, and letter disc on top with careful height offsets so nothing clips through the rim.

Setting the rim torus position and dimensions, then defining each bar's start and end points radiating outward from the deck center based on angle θ, with target tips arcing upward and outward.

I'm adding small details—a pivot sphere at each bar's base and a chrome slug at the tip—plus thinking through the plinth logo stripe and the wedge-shaped bed geometry, working out how rotating and translating the extruded shape maps its local coordinates into the final centered position.
